x.A: KMS stores encryption keys and can't store and return database credentials for the application to use.
x.B: Encrypted local storage with a cron job rotation means building and maintaining the rotation yourself, and the credentials stay on the server.
x.C: Secrets Manager stores the database credentials, the application loads them with a small code change, and it rotates the RDS for MySQL credentials automatically through a managed rotation function.
x.D: Parameter Store has no built-in rotation of RDS credentials.

x.A: A new bucket with SSE-KMS using multi-Region keys and CRR keeps encrypted copies in two Regions, and loading the data into the new bucket means all of it is replicated. Athena queries it with SQL and is serverless.
x.B: RDS isn't serverless, and querying data in S3 with it needs the data loaded into a database.
x.C: CRR replicates only objects added after it's enabled, so the existing data wouldn't be copied to the other Region.
x.D: CRR doesn't copy existing objects, and RDS isn't serverless or a way to query S3 data.

x.A: Uploaded images used for training twice a year go to Glacier Deep Archive, the cheapest class. Premium users' generated images that can be downloaded anytime stay in Standard, and non-premium images, which are accessed rarely (once every 6 hours at most), go to Standard-IA.
x.B: Generated images in Glacier Flexible Retrieval aren't immediately available, so premium users couldn't download them anytime.
x.C: One Zone-IA for uploaded images costs more than Deep Archive for data used just twice a year, and training doesn't need immediate access.
x.D: Putting all generated images in Glacier Flexible Retrieval doesn't allow premium users to download them anytime.

x.A: An NLB can't invoke Lambda functions, and Lambda isn't suited to loading 1 GB of model data at startup for each request. Lambda also doesn't scale by network load balancer traffic.
x.B: An ALB handles synchronous requests, and the usage is an asynchronous API with irregular batches, so a queue is a better fit. Scaling by ALB traffic isn't as accurate.
x.C: You can't scale the vCPUs of a Lambda function with auto scaling, and Lambda isn't a good fit for loading 1 GB at each start.
x.D: SQS holds requests durably for the asynchronous API, and ECS services load the model once and read from the queue. Auto scaling on the queue size scales up for batches and down to zero when models aren't used.

x.A: A scaled-down (pilot light/warm standby) environment in a second Region with a minimal Auto Scaling group, an Aurora global database, and Route 53 active-passive failover meets the 30 minute recovery time, and it doesn't serve traffic when the primary is healthy.
x.B: Active-active failover serves customers from both Regions and the Auto Scaling group can't span Regions, so this doesn't fit.
x.C: Restoring a backup into a new Aurora cluster takes longer than 30 minutes, and active-active isn't needed.
x.D: Rebuilding the infrastructure from a backup with zero desired capacity makes recovery slower than the requirement.

x.A: Spot Instances can be interrupted, but the batch jobs can't be disrupted. Glacier Instant Retrieval costs more than Deep Archive for data only kept after 30 days.
x.B: Storing data directly in Glacier Instant Retrieval right after the jobs makes data accessible for 30 days at a higher price than S3 Standard for the access, and the move to Deep Archive adds cost.
x.C: Spot Instances can be interrupted, which isn't acceptable for jobs that can't be disrupted, and Flexible Retrieval costs more than Deep Archive.
x.D: On-Demand Instances avoid interruptions for the jobs, S3 Standard serves the data for 30 days, and Glacier Deep Archive is the cheapest for retention until it's deleted at 2 years.

x.A: A Site-to-Site VPN to each VPC goes over the internet, so it can't give consistent single-digit latency, and it needs a connection to each VPC.
x.B: Associating a Direct Connect gateway with the transit gateway connects the on-premises network to all VPCs attached to the transit gateway through Direct Connect.
x.C: A VPN to a Direct Connect gateway isn't a valid setup, and VPN latency isn't consistent.
x.D: A Direct Connect connection with a transit virtual interface to a Direct Connect gateway gives a private, low-latency link to the transit gateway.
x.E: VPN connections run over the internet, so latency is inconsistent and can't meet single-digit latency.

x.A: RDS Proxy keeps application connections open and routes them to the new primary after a failover, which shortens the failover time customers see and reduces timeouts.
x.B: A read replica takes read traffic but doesn't shorten the failover time of the primary.
x.C: Performance Insights shows load but doesn't speed up failover.
x.D: Snapshots and copies to other Regions help with backups and don't affect failover time.

x.A: A CloudWatch alarm can't identify instances to stop by schedule, and it needs a Lambda function, so it has more overhead.
x.B: Trusted Advisor reports don't start and stop instances by schedule, so it needs extra work.
x.C: Systems Manager State Manager associations can run Automation documents on a schedule to start and stop RDS instances identified by tags, with no code.
x.D: EventBridge rules with Lambda functions work but require writing and maintaining code.

x.A: Requester Pays makes the marketing firm pay the request and data transfer charges for its own downloads, so the company's transfer costs are minimized.
x.B: CRR makes the company pay for replication and data transfer between Regions, which raises its costs.
x.C: Sharing with Resource Access Manager doesn't change who pays data transfer costs.
x.D: Intelligent-Tiering reduces storage cost and doesn't reduce data transfer costs, and syncing the bucket makes the company pay for the transfer.

x.A: AWS WAF can't be associated with a Global Accelerator accelerator.
x.B: A Lambda function reading ALB metrics and updating network ACLs is custom code to build and maintain, and ACLs can't handle large attacks.
x.C: AWS WAF on the ALB with rate-based rules blocks IP addresses that send too many requests, which mitigates the DDoS attack with the least effort.
x.D: CloudFront in front of Global Accelerator isn't a supported pattern and adds more architecture changes.

x.A: The Athena DynamoDB connector queries the table directly with Lambda, which consumes read capacity on the table, so it affects the website's provisioned capacity.
x.B: A Glue job with the DynamoDB export connector reads from a table export (using point-in-time recovery) in S3, so it doesn't consume the table's read capacity.
x.C: Redshift COPY reads directly from the DynamoDB table and uses its read capacity.
x.D: A Hive external table on EMR scans the DynamoDB table directly, which uses its read capacity.

x.A: SNS doesn't store jobs durably for processing, and CPU usage isn't a good scaling metric for the number of jobs.
x.B: SQS stores jobs durably, but network usage isn't a good indicator of the number of jobs to process.
x.C: SQS holds the jobs durably and loosely couples the application. An Auto Scaling group using the launch template scales on the number of items in the queue, so instances are added and removed as needed.
x.D: SNS doesn't hold jobs durably, and the number of messages published isn't a good scaling signal.

x.A: RDS isn't a good place to store product images, and a fixed EC2 instance with Auto Scaling needs more management than Fargate.
x.B: Running a monolith in Lambda isn't modular, DynamoDB doesn't keep structured schemas, and it isn't a good place for images.
x.C: EKS on EC2 means managing nodes, and Glacier Deep Archive isn't suitable for product images that are served to customers.
x.D: ECS on Fargate runs the modular containerized services without servers, RDS Multi-AZ keeps the structured schemas, and S3 stores the images. It has the least operational overhead.

x.A: Client-side encryption with customer managed keys encrypts the data before it's sent to S3, so the data is already encrypted when stored.
x.B: Server-side encryption encrypts the data after S3 receives it, not before storing, so it doesn't meet the requirement to encrypt before sending.
x.C: SSE-C is also server-side, so the data is encrypted after S3 receives it.
x.D: S3 managed keys are used for server-side encryption, so client-side encryption with S3 managed keys isn't possible.

x.A: Interface endpoints control network paths to AWS services but don't give each team's workloads separate permissions, and don't block access to IMDSv2.
x.B: EMR runtime roles give each job its own IAM role with only the permissions the team needs, and workloads don't use the instance profile credentials from the instance metadata service, so teams only access the services they need.
x.C: An instance profile applies to the whole instance, so all workloads on it would share permissions and could access the instance metadata.
x.D: A security configuration with EnableApplicationScopedIAMRole set to false doesn't give each team its own permissions.

x.A: An SQS FIFO queue stores form data durably, delivers each message exactly once and in order, and the worker tier processes it quickly, so no data is lost.
x.B: An API Gateway HTTP API doesn't store and forward data and doesn't guarantee exactly-once processing.
x.C: A standard queue gives at-least-once delivery, so a form could be processed more than once.
x.D: A synchronous Step Functions workflow doesn't store and forward in a durable queue and can lose data if the worker fails.

x.A: EC2 instances to ingest streams means managing servers, and Athena isn't a real-time search service.
x.B: EMR and Redshift aren't built for real-time updates to search features.
x.C: EKS to ingest and CloudWatch dashboards to search data isn't a real-time search and visualization solution.
x.D: Kinesis Data Streams ingests the streaming data in real time, OpenSearch Service provides real-time search, and QuickSight visualizes the data. All are AWS native managed services.

x.A: App2Container containerizes the ASP.NET application, and deploying it with CloudFormation to ECS on Fargate means no servers to manage and scaling with CloudWatch metrics. It has the least operational overhead.
x.B: ECS on EC2 means managing the instances, which adds operational work.
x.C: App Runner doesn't containerize an existing application, and it doesn't deploy to ECS.
x.D: App Runner doesn't deploy to EKS, and EKS on EC2 is more operational overhead.

x.A: Parameter Store isn't the managed service made for storing and retrieving multiple secrets with the BatchGetSecretValue API, which belongs to Secrets Manager.
x.B: Adding AWS Batch is an unnecessary service for retrieving secrets.
x.C: Parameter Store doesn't have the BatchGetSecretValue API, and AWS Batch isn't needed.
x.D: Secrets Manager securely stores credentials, and the BatchGetSecretValue API retrieves multiple secrets in one call. Using CloudFormation to integrate it needs the least operational overhead.

x.A: A CachingDisabled policy means CloudFront doesn't cache the files, so every download goes to the origin, which doesn't reduce latency.
x.B: A second bucket and replication adds more operational work, and a secondary origin is only for failover, not for lowering latency.
x.C: S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads and downloads for single objects, but for 100 files across thousands of servers, caching at the edge is better.
x.D: CloudFront caches the software files at edge locations near the Outposts servers around the world, which reduces deployment latency, and signed URLs control access. It needs the least operational work.

x.A: A Windows Server cluster with FSx for Windows File Server provides file storage, not block storage, and takes more setup.
x.B: Application-level replication between two EBS volumes in different AZs is complex to set up and manage.
x.C: FSx for NetApp ONTAP Multi-AZ provides block storage over iSCSI that is replicated across AZs with low latency. An active and standby instance with it needs the least implementation effort.
x.D: EBS volumes can't replicate across AZs at the EBS level, so this isn't possible.

x.A: The ALB's security group must allow inbound HTTPS on 443 from anywhere to receive public web traffic.
x.B: Allowing all outbound traffic on 443 to anywhere is broader than needed. The ALB should send traffic only to the web application instances.
x.C: The ALB needs outbound HTTPS to the web application instances on port 443 to forward requests.
x.D: Inbound traffic from the web servers isn't needed, because security groups are stateful and return traffic is allowed automatically.
x.E: The ALB needs outbound HTTPS to the web application instances on port 8443 to run the health checks.
x.F: Inbound traffic from the instances for the health check isn't needed, because the ALB initiates the checks and replies are allowed automatically.

x.A: CloudFront requires the ACM certificate to be in us-east-1 for a custom domain name, regardless of where the S3 bucket is.
x.B: A certificate in eu-west-1 can't be used with CloudFront.
x.C: Transfer Acceleration isn't needed with CloudFront, and it doesn't set up access from CloudFront.
x.D: CloudFront origin access control (OAC) lets the S3 bucket accept uploads (PUT requests) only from the CloudFront distribution, keeping the bucket private.
x.E: An S3 website endpoint doesn't support OAC and isn't needed for uploads.

x.A: Athena queries Parquet files in S3 with standard SQL, can read files encrypted with client-side KMS encryption (CSE-KMS), and bills per query, which suits occasional queries on a specific day's prefix.
x.B: S3 Select doesn't support client-side encrypted objects and is limited to a single object at a time, and it's no longer available to new customers.
x.C: Redshift Spectrum needs a Redshift cluster running, which costs more for occasional queries.
x.D: EMR Serverless works but costs more and takes more setup than Athena for occasional queries.
